section_title: How does the Father draw people to the living bread?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 41 At this, the Jews began to grumble about Jesus because He had said, “I am the bread that came down from heaven.” 42 They were asking, “Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then can He say, ‘I have come down from heaven’ ?” 43 “Stop grumbling among yourselves,” Jesus replied. 44 “No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him, and I will raise him up at the last day. 45 It is written in the Prophets: ‘And they will all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard the Father and learned from Him comes to Me— 46 not that anyone has seen the Father except the One who is from God; only He has seen the Father.

47 Truly, truly, I tell you, he who believes has eternal life. 48 I am the bread of life. 49 Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, yet they died. 50 This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that anyone may eat of it and not die. 51 I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And this bread, which I will give for the life of the world, is My flesh.”

context_lines: Some of Jesus’ hearers grumble because He says He has come from heaven. They think they know His family, so His claim does not fit what they assume about Him. Jesus answers by speaking of the Father drawing people to Him and teaching them.

The Greek verb behind drawing is ἕλκω, helkō (HEL-koh). Thayer lists physical pulling or hauling among its uses, and also lists the inward leading described here. That figurative use helps explain why Jesus immediately speaks about hearing and learning from the Father. ([Thayer, Greek 1670](https://biblehub.com/greek/1670.htm))

Jesus quotes the promise that people will be taught by God, then distinguishes His own knowledge of the Father from theirs. He repeats that the believer has eternal life and contrasts the manna eaten by ancestors who died with the living bread He gives. He identifies that gift with His flesh given for the life of the world.
common_interpretation_lines: Christian traditions agree that coming to Christ depends on God’s grace. Where traditions differ is how His drawing works in a person’s response.

Reformed teaching in the Westminster Confession says that God changes the hearts of those He calls so that they freely and willingly come to Christ. Calvin likewise reads this as an inward work that brings about the response, rather than external force against a person who remains unwilling. ([Westminster Confession 10.1–2](https://www.opc.org/wcf.html); [Calvin on John 6:44](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/john/6.htm))

Wesley teaches that God first gives the ability and desire to respond, while allowing that this grace can be resisted. The Catholic Catechism also places the beginning entirely in God’s undeserved initiative, while teaching that His initiative calls for a free human response. These readings differ from saying that a person can come to Christ without God first acting. ([Wesley on John 6:44](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-john/); [Catechism §§1996–2002](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_three/section_one/chapter_three/article_2/ii_grace.index.html))
god_plan_lines: Jesus explicitly connects His teaching with Isaiah’s promise that the children of God’s restored people will be taught by the Lord. Isaiah places that promise alongside God’s enduring love and covenant of peace. The Father’s teaching here belongs within that scriptural hope of a people restored and taught by Him. ([Isaiah 54:10–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/isaiah/54.htm); [John 6:45](https://biblehub.com/bsb/john/6.htm))

Ephesians describes God’s purpose in Christ as bringing people into His family, making them holy, and giving forgiveness through the Son. That provides a wider account of what His gracious initiative is for: life with Him as His children, to the praise of His grace. ([Ephesians 1:3–10](https://biblehub.com/bsb/ephesians/1.htm))
current_position_lines: Our study Prayer and Faith reads Jesus as the living bread to whom the manna pointed. The manna sustained life for a time; Christ Himself gives lasting life. The study connects receiving that life with faith and continued dependence on Him.

editorial_review.position_source_detail: Prayer and Faith: Section4 The Missing Link — Christ as the Living Bread; direct developed John6:32–58/48–51/58 discussion. Narrow Christ-as-life/bread/faith/dependence conclusion, not a new ruling on drawing, perseverance or Eucharistic presence.
